questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a General Polynomial
questions.problem:
Consider the quadratic function $f(x)=4-{x}^{2}.$

Current part:

Find ${lim}_{x\to \,\infty }f(x).$ If the limit does not exist, write "DNE" (without the quotation marks).

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${lim}_{x\to \,\infty }f(x)=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We identify the leading term of the polynomial and compute its limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }(4-{x}^{2}) & ={lim}_{x\to \,\infty }(-{x}^{2}) \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }({x}^{2}) \\  & =-(\infty ) \\  & =-\infty \end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
questions.problem:
Consider the quadratic function $f(x)=4-{x}^{2}.$

Earlier part 1:

Find ${lim}_{x\to \,\infty }f(x).$ If the limit does not exist, write "DNE" (without the quotation marks).

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${lim}_{x\to \,\infty }f(x)=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        $-\infty$

Current part:

Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{x}}{f(x)}.$ If the limit does not exist, write "DNE" (without the quotation marks).

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{x}}{f(x)}=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit directly by substituting $x=2,$ we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{x}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{x}}{4-{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2}}{4-{2}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since there is a radical in the numerator, we can evaluate the limit by first multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{x}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{x}}{4-{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{(\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{x})(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x})}{(4-{x}^{2})(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{2-x}{(2+x)(2-x)(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\cancel{2-x}}{(2+x)\cancel{(2-x)}(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{1}{(2+x)(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{x})} \\  & =\frac{1}{(2+2)(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{4(2\sqrt{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{8\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13950896/assets/e13444351bb092ced6fc788ae921622f154a267e9544e928700736a53a259fc6.png)

The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the right Riemann sum with step size $Δx=0.5,$ as follows:

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0.5)+f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3.75$ | $3$ | $1.75$ | $0$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3.75+3+1.75+0)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =8.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =4.25\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The right Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$ 

In our case, we have $n=4$ subintervals, $a=0,$ $b=2,$ and $Δx=0.5.$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the right Riemann sum can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f(a+iΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}f(0+i\cdot 0.5)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}f(0.5i) \\  & =0.5{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}(4-{(0.5i)}^{2}) \\  & =0.5{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}(4-0.25{i}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the area $A$ as the definite integral of 

$$
f(x)=4-{x}^{2}
$$

between 

* the lower limit $x=0,$ and 

* the upper limit $x=2.$ 

This gives

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{2}4-{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$
